newsitem.title: USA: U.S. SEC's new derivatives rule faces key hurdle.
newsitem.headline: U.S. SEC's new derivatives rule faces key hurdle.

text.p: Two key Republicans are considering whether or not to overturn a new Securities and Exchange Commission rule requiring firms to disclose more information about the derivatives they hold.

Rep. David McIntosh of Indiana, who chairs the regulatory subcommittee of the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee, and Texas Senator Phil Gramm, have until the end of this month to introduce a resolution under the Congressional Review Act if they want to abolish the rules quickly, Congressional aides said in interviews late last week.
"McIntosh is seriously considering that and he and Gramm will make a decision by the end of April," an aide to McIntosh's committee said.

Gramm, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee's securities subcommittee, first indicated last month that his panel may opt to override the agency's rules. At that time, he faulted the agency's in its review of the rule's potential impact on firms.
"We haven't dismissed that possiblity. We would hope that we can get it resolved without having to resort to that but that is of course one of the approaches you can go with," a Senate aide said.
Meanwhile, to help stall those efforts, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt has vowed to make better use of the agency's economists when designing new regulations.

"I have already taken steps to ensure that the Commission's Office of Economic Analysis is consulted at an early stage of all regulatory intitiatives," Levitt promised Phil Gramm, the Texas Senator who chairs Senate Banking Committee's securities subcommittee, in an April 9 letter.
But it is not clear whether or not Levitt's latest offering is enough to stall Gramm and McIntosh of Indiana.
Staff on the House oversight committee were disappointed with the explanations the SEC's chief economist and chief accountant provided in special interviews held earlier this month.
"The initial economic analysis appears to be largely guess work and their final economic analysis appears to be based largely on anecdotal conversations," an aide to McIntosh's subcommittee said.
The new disclosure rules require, among other things, additional information from firms that includes potential value changes according to risk models.

The rules, which are widely opposed, even from within the agency, have put the SEC in the hot seat with lawmakers, particularly in light of strong criticism by the agency's chief economist about the impact of the disclosure rules.

"I am most troubled that the chief economist's conclusions, and many other comments that the SEC received from the regulated community on the quantitative disclosure requirements, appear to have been completely ignored," McIntosh wrote in a letter to Levitt late last month.

The lawmakers are also bothered that Levitt in a speech last year to the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, tried to discourage the industry from lobbying Congress about pending accounting rules, aides said.
"For Chairman Levitt to implicitly make such threats is an interference of our oversight powers at a minimum and it's offensive no matter which way you look at it," a Congressional aide said.
